::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## At a glance

**Guiding question:** What separates a biological signal from illumination and device characteristics?\
**For:** doctoral researchers and preclinical teams who analyse spectral images, and reviewers of such studies. ·
**Prerequisites:** analysis units and denominators from @sec-b03; baseline thinking from @sec-b05.\
**In the course:** [W4 · What imaging, gait and tissue models
measure](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w4-imaging-gait-tissue.html) ·
**Data:** synthetic (generated in the chapter; fictitious animals) · **Core reading time:** about 10 minutes
:::

## Case and decision {#sec-b10-case}

A doctoral researcher in a fictitious preclinical group analyses hyperspectral images of skin flaps in eight rats. The
question is whether a fictitious substance improves the oxygenation of the flap tip on day 3. The four control animals
were imaged in the first week, the four treated animals in the second. Between the two weeks the camera lamp was
replaced. The camera records a new white reference at every start-up, but the analysis script still loads the file
from the first day. The oxygenation index of the treated animals is clearly higher, and a t-test over all pixels
returns a p-value far below 0.001. The supervisor wants to submit an abstract this week. The researcher has to decide
whether to report a treatment effect, or first to check the calibration and count how many independent units the
study really has. The first error in this chapter is not statistical. It is the light.

## Core reading {#sec-b10-core}

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Core reading** · required for W4 · about 10 minutes · ends before ‘Lab’
:::

**What the camera records.** A hyperspectral camera stores a cube of numbers: two spatial axes and one spectral axis.
Every pixel holds a spectrum, here 101 values from 500 to 1,000 nm in steps of 5 nm. The raw value in each band is a
count from the sensor (digital numbers, DN). It is the product of three things: how much light the lamp emits at that
wavelength, how much of it the tissue reflects, and how sensitive the sensor is at that wavelength. Only the middle
factor is biology [@lu2014hsi].

**Calibration turns counts into reflectance.** Two reference images separate the tissue from the device. A dark
reference, taken with the shutter closed, records the sensor's offset. A white reference, taken of a standard tile that
reflects almost all light (here 99%), records lamp and sensor together. The reflectance of a pixel is then
$R(\lambda) = 0.99 \cdot (\text{raw} - \text{dark}) / (\text{white} - \text{dark})$, a dimensionless share between 0
and 1. **The key assumption is that the white reference was recorded under the same light as the tissue image.** If
the lamp changes in between, the division no longer cancels it.

**From spectrum to index.** Deoxygenated haemoglobin absorbs red light around 660 nm much more strongly than
oxygenated haemoglobin, whereas around 800 nm the two absorb similarly. The ratio $R(660)/R(800)$ therefore rises
with oxygenation. Real perfusion parameters are more elaborate and are derived from validated absorption models
[@holmer2018hsi]; the index in this chapter is a didactic simplification built on synthetic absorption profiles. A
ratio has one useful property: it cancels anything that scales the whole spectrum, such as the distance between camera
and tissue. It does not cancel anything that changes the *shape* of the spectrum.

**Two kinds of reference.** The word "reference" means two different things in this chapter. The white and dark
references are *technical* references: they turn the number on the screen into a reflectance, and a grey tile of known
reflectance can check them at every session. A *biological* reference answers another question: does the index track
tissue oxygenation at all? That would need an independent measurement in the same tissue, for example an invasive
oxygen probe or a histological marker of ischaemia, read without knowledge of the index. The synthetic study has no
such reference; its absence is recorded as *open*. Without it, a higher index means "the tissue reflects relatively
more red light", not "the tissue is better oxygenated". The physical units change along the chain: wavelength in
nanometres, raw signal in counts, reflectance as a share between 0 and 1, and the index as a dimensionless ratio. A
difference of 0.05 index units has no clinical meaning until a biological reference has given it one.


::: {.cell}

:::


**What went wrong.** The replacement lamp is brighter and emits relatively more red light. Brightness alone would not
matter for a ratio. The change in colour does: with the old white reference, the reflectance at 660 nm is inflated
relative to 800 nm by a factor of 1.117, and so is every index measured in week 2 (*synthetic*).
Because all treated animals were imaged in week 2, lamp and treatment are completely confounded. No statistical model
can separate them; only a calibration with the matching white reference can. A gain of about
12% is roughly the difference between the poorly perfused tip and the well perfused base of
a flap in the synthetic data, so the artefact is large enough to look like biology.

**The measurement chain.** @fig-b10-chain lays out each step from lamp to decision. It marks where the references
enter, where the physical unit changes and where a learning model could replace the simple index. Drawing the chain
before analysing data is the quickest way to find the step at which a device property can masquerade as a treatment
effect.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
library(ggplot2)
# Generic drawing of a measurement chain: one box per step, a note per step, dashed border for the learning model
draw_chain <- function(steps, note_title = "Unit or reference") {
  steps$y <- rev(seq_len(nrow(steps)))
  types <- c("measurement", "reference", "model", "decision")
  ggplot(steps) +
    geom_segment(data = steps[-nrow(steps), ], aes(x = 1, xend = 1, y = y - 0.24, yend = y - 0.76),
                 arrow = grid::arrow(length = grid::unit(0.15, "cm")), colour = "grey30") +
    geom_tile(aes(x = 1, y = y, fill = type, linetype = type), width = 1.7, height = 0.5,
              colour = "grey20", linewidth = 0.5) +
    geom_text(aes(x = 1, y = y, label = label), size = 3.4) +
    geom_text(aes(x = 2.0, y = y, label = note), hjust = 0, size = 3.1, colour = "grey15") +
    annotate("text", x = 2.0, y = nrow(steps) + 0.55, label = note_title, hjust = 0, fontface = "bold",
             size = 3.2) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(measurement = "white", reference = "grey85", model = "#D9ECF7",
                                 decision = "grey70"), breaks = types, name = NULL) +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = c(measurement = "solid", reference = "solid", model = "dashed",
                                     decision = "solid"), breaks = types, name = NULL) +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0.1, 4.6)) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0.5, nrow(steps) + 0.8)) +
    theme_void(base_size = 11) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, colour = "#4D4D4D"))
}
chain_b10 <- data.frame(
  label = c("Lamp and tissue", "Camera: raw counts", "Dark and white reference", "Reflectance spectrum (pixel)",
            "Region mean (acquisition)", "Index or learning model", "Animal mean", "Group comparison, decision"),
  note = c("wavelength 500-1,000 nm; lamp spectrum varies", "counts (DN) per band",
           "white tile 99% reflectance; same lamp required", "share 0-1, dimensionless; 1,200 pixels per run",
           "48 region means (8 animals x 2 regions x 3)", "index R(660)/R(800); model on 101 bands",
           "independent unit: animal, n = 8", "4 vs 4 animals; check order of imaging"),
  type = c("measurement", "measurement", "reference", "measurement", "measurement", "model", "measurement",
           "decision")
)
draw_chain(chain_b10) +
  labs(caption = "Synthetic case · fictitious animals · independent unit: animal (n = 8)")
```

**Count the units before testing.** The study produces many numbers, but few independent ones (@tbl-b10-units).
Pixels within one region share the same animal, the same lamp and the same acquisition; they are pseudoreplicates, not
replicates [@lazic2010pseudoreplication]. The experimental unit is the animal, as the ARRIVE guidelines ask authors to
state explicitly [@percie2020arrive].

| Level | Count in the case | What varies at this level | Unit for the treatment test? |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Pixel | 1,200 (8 × 2 × 3 × 25) | noise, small-scale tissue texture | no |
| Region in one acquisition | 48 | positioning, brightness | no |
| Animal | 8 (4 per group) | biology, treatment | **yes** |
| Imaging week | 2 | lamp, calibration file | confounded with group |

: Analysis levels in the hyperspectral case. Synthetic design; independent unit for the treatment question: animal (n = 8). {#tbl-b10-units}

**Where the learning model sits.** A classifier trained on full spectra could replace the index in step six of the
chain, for instance to tell well and poorly perfused tissue apart. It sits *after* calibration and inherits every
calibration error. It therefore has to be compared with the simple index on new animals, not on new pixels of known
animals, and it has to pass the same illumination check.

**Question for the workshop:** Which single additional image, taken at every imaging session, would have revealed the
lamp problem before any animal was analysed, and what value would you expect it to show?

## Lab {#sec-b10-lab}

The lab simulates the whole chain: synthetic tissue spectra, lamp, sensor, dark and white references, calibration, the
index, a grouped test and a comparison of the index with a learning model on new animals. All absorption profiles are
synthetic and qualitative; they are not tabulated extinction coefficients.

**Step 1 – tissue, lamps and sensor.**


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
wl <- seq(500, 1000, by = 5)                      # wavelengths in nm (101 bands)
bump <- function(centre, width) exp(-0.5 * ((wl - centre) / width)^2)
# Synthetic absorption profiles: deoxygenated absorbs strongly around 660 nm, both are similar near 800 nm
abs_deoxy <- 1.00 * bump(555, 22) + 0.32 * bump(650, 60) + 0.10 * bump(760, 14) + 0.06
abs_oxy   <- 0.85 * bump(542, 11) + 0.90 * bump(577, 10) + 0.05 * bump(900, 90) + 0.06
# Tissue reflectance (share 0-1) for oxygen saturation 'sat', blood volume factor and scattering factor
tissue_reflectance <- function(sat, blood, scatter = 1) {
  background <- (0.55 + 0.00025 * (wl - 500)) * scatter
  background * exp(-blood * (sat * abs_oxy + (1 - sat) * abs_deoxy))
}
lamp_A <- 0.45 + 0.55 * (wl - 500) / 500                  # original lamp, rising towards the infrared
lamp_B <- 1.2 * lamp_A * (1 + 0.25 * (800 - wl) / 300)    # replacement: 20% brighter, relatively more red
sensor <- 0.95 - 0.45 * ((wl - 720) / 300)^2              # relative sensor sensitivity
full_scale <- 20000                                       # counts for a perfect reflector
dark_level <- 300                                         # sensor offset in counts
# Raw counts of one spectrum: signal plus offset plus photon noise
raw_counts <- function(reflectance, lamp) {
  signal <- full_scale * lamp * sensor * reflectance
  signal + dark_level + rnorm(length(signal), 0, sqrt(signal + dark_level))
}
# Index of one spectrum (vector) or of every pixel (matrix with one column per pixel)
oxygen_index <- function(R) {
  if (is.matrix(R)) R[wl == 660, ] / R[wl == 800, ] else R[wl == 660] / R[wl == 800]
}
round(c(poorly_oxygenated = oxygen_index(tissue_reflectance(0.45, 1.5)),
        well_oxygenated = oxygen_index(tissue_reflectance(0.70, 1.5))), 3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> poorly_oxygenated   well_oxygenated 
#>             0.750             0.847
```


:::
:::


**Step 2 – dark and white references and a check.** The white reference is the mean of ten frames of the 99% tile
under each lamp. A grey tile with a flat reflectance of 50% serves as a check: after calibration its spectrum must be
flat at 0.5 and its index must be 1.00 within a tolerance of ±0.02, set before the study (*assumption*).


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(1010)
lamps <- list(week1 = lamp_A, week2 = lamp_B)
white_ref <- lapply(lamps, function(l) rowMeans(sapply(1:10, function(i) raw_counts(rep(0.99, length(wl)), l))))
calibrate <- function(raw, white) 0.99 * (raw - dark_level) / (white - dark_level)
# Grey check tile: mean of 100 pixels, calibrated with the matching and with the stale white reference
grey_tile <- function(week, white) {
  raw <- sapply(1:100, function(i) raw_counts(rep(0.50, length(wl)), lamps[[week]]))
  rowMeans(calibrate(raw, white))
}
check <- data.frame(
  week = c("week 1", "week 2", "week 2"),
  white_reference = c("matching", "matching", "stale (week 1)"),
  mean_reflectance = c(mean(grey_tile(1, white_ref$week1)), mean(grey_tile(2, white_ref$week2)),
                       mean(grey_tile(2, white_ref$week1))),
  grey_index = c(oxygen_index(grey_tile(1, white_ref$week1)), oxygen_index(grey_tile(2, white_ref$week2)),
                 oxygen_index(grey_tile(2, white_ref$week1)))
)
check$within_tolerance <- abs(check$grey_index - 1) <= 0.02
check
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>     week white_reference mean_reflectance grey_index within_tolerance
#> 1 week 1        matching        0.5000383  0.9945404             TRUE
#> 2 week 2        matching        0.5000635  0.9912745             TRUE
#> 3 week 2  stale (week 1)        0.6251338  1.1137797            FALSE
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
stopifnot(check$within_tolerance == c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE),
          abs(check$mean_reflectance[1:2] - 0.5) < 0.01)
```
:::


The stale white reference fails the grey check in week 2. The check needs no animal and no statistics.

**Step 3 – eight fictitious animals.** In the synthetic truth the substance has no effect: both groups draw their
oxygen saturation from the same distribution. Each animal has two regions (flap base and flap tip), three acquisitions
per region and 25 pixels per region of interest.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(2018)
animals <- data.frame(animal = sprintf("R%02d", 1:8), group = rep(c("control", "treatment"), each = 4),
                      week = rep(1:2, each = 4))
animals$blood <- rnorm(8, 1.5, 0.15)                       # blood volume factor per animal
animals$scatter <- rnorm(8, 1, 0.05)                       # scattering factor per animal
animals$sat_base <- rnorm(8, 0.70, 0.03)                   # no treatment effect in the synthetic truth
animals$sat_tip <- animals$sat_base - rnorm(8, 0.25, 0.03) # the tip is less well perfused
pixel_rows <- list()
spectrum_rows <- list()
for (a in 1:8) for (region in c("base", "tip")) for (acq in 1:3) {
  sat <- if (region == "base") animals$sat_base[a] else animals$sat_tip[a]
  sat_acq <- sat + rnorm(1, 0, 0.01)                       # small change between acquisitions
  brightness <- rnorm(1, 1, 0.05)                          # distance and angle change the overall level
  raw <- sapply(1:25, function(p) raw_counts(
    brightness * tissue_reflectance(sat_acq + rnorm(1, 0, 0.02), animals$blood[a], animals$scatter[a]),
    lamps[[animals$week[a]]]))
  for (cal in c("stale", "matching")) {
    white <- if (cal == "matching") white_ref[[animals$week[a]]] else white_ref$week1
    R <- calibrate(raw, white)                              # 101 bands x 25 pixels
    info <- data.frame(animal = animals$animal[a], group = animals$group[a], week = animals$week[a],
                       region = region, acquisition = acq, calibration = cal)
    pixel_rows[[length(pixel_rows) + 1]] <- cbind(info, pixel = 1:25, index = oxygen_index(R))
    spectrum_rows[[length(spectrum_rows) + 1]] <- cbind(info, t(rowMeans(R)))
  }
}
pixels <- do.call(rbind, pixel_rows)
spectra <- do.call(rbind, spectrum_rows)
names(spectra)[-(1:6)] <- paste0("nm", wl)
spectra$index <- spectra$nm660 / spectra$nm800
c(pixels_per_calibration = nrow(pixels) / 2, region_means = nrow(spectra) / 2, animals = nrow(animals))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> pixels_per_calibration           region_means                animals 
#>                   1200                     48                      8
```


:::
:::


**Step 4 – the grouped test.** The treatment question concerns the flap tip. We test it twice, once with every pixel as
if it were independent and once with one mean per animal, and we do this for both calibrations.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tip <- pixels[pixels$region == "tip", ]
grouped_tests <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("stale", "matching"), function(cal) {
  d <- tip[tip$calibration == cal, ]
  per_animal <- aggregate(index ~ animal + group, data = d, FUN = mean)   # one value per animal
  data.frame(calibration = cal,
             n_pixels = nrow(d), p_pixels = t.test(index ~ group, data = d)$p.value,
             n_animals = nrow(per_animal), p_animals = t.test(index ~ group, data = per_animal)$p.value,
             mean_control = mean(per_animal$index[per_animal$group == "control"]),
             mean_treatment = mean(per_animal$index[per_animal$group == "treatment"]))
}))
grouped_tests
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>   calibration n_pixels      p_pixels n_animals   p_animals mean_control
#> 1       stale      600 5.340962e-173         8 0.001330005    0.7544171
#> 2    matching      600  3.513837e-12         8 0.352695787    0.7544171
#>   mean_treatment
#> 1      0.8313038
#> 2      0.7416595
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
stopifnot(
  grouped_tests$n_animals == 8,
  grouped_tests$p_pixels < 0.001,                              # pixel tests are 'significant' in both cases
  grouped_tests$p_animals[grouped_tests$calibration == "stale"] < 0.05,
  grouped_tests$p_animals[grouped_tests$calibration == "matching"] > 0.05
)
```
:::


Two lessons sit in this table. With the stale white reference, the "effect" survives even the correct animal-level
test (p = 0.0013 with 4 vs 4 animals): the right denominator does not protect
against confounding. With the matching reference the mean index of the treated animals is
0.013 index units
lower than that of the
controls, and the animal-level test gives p = 0.35. The pixel-level test still
reports p = 3.5e-12 for this chance difference, because it
treats 600 tip pixels from eight animals as 600 independent
observations. @fig-b10-index shows both levels.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
acq_tip <- spectra[spectra$region == "tip", ]
animal_tip <- aggregate(index ~ animal + group + calibration, data = acq_tip, FUN = mean)
facet_names <- c(stale = "Stale white reference (week 1)", matching = "Matching white reference")
acq_tip$calibration <- factor(facet_names[acq_tip$calibration], levels = facet_names)
animal_tip$calibration <- factor(facet_names[animal_tip$calibration], levels = facet_names)
ggplot(acq_tip, aes(group, index, colour = group, shape = group)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.12, height = 0, seed = 1), size = 1.4, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(data = animal_tip, size = 3.6, position = position_jitter(width = 0.12, height = 0, seed = 2)) +
  facet_wrap(~ calibration) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(cdsr_colours[c("blue", "orange")])) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = cdsr_shapes[1:2]) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Oxygenation index R(660)/R(800) (dimensionless)", colour = NULL, shape = NULL,
       caption = "Synthetic data · flap tip · n = 8 animals (4 per group), 3 acquisitions each") +
  theme_cdsr()
```

**Step 5 – index against a learning model on new animals.** Before a learning model earns a place in the chain, it
has to beat the simple index on animals it has never seen. We develop both methods on the four week-1 animals and test
them on the four week-2 animals. The model is a k-nearest-neighbour classifier (k = 3) on the first three principal
components of the full region-mean spectra; the principal components are computed from the training animals only. The
task is to tell flap base from flap tip.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(class)
bands <- paste0("nm", wl)
train <- spectra[spectra$week == 1 & spectra$calibration == "matching", ]
# Index baseline: threshold halfway between the mean index of base and tip in the training animals
threshold <- mean(tapply(train$index, train$region, mean))
# Learning model: principal components from training spectra only, then k-nearest neighbours
pca <- prcomp(train[, bands], center = TRUE)
evaluate <- function(cal) {
  test <- spectra[spectra$week == 2 & spectra$calibration == cal, ]
  pred_index <- ifelse(test$index > threshold, "base", "tip")
  scores_test <- predict(pca, test[, bands])[, 1:3]
  pred_model <- as.character(knn(pca$x[, 1:3], scores_test, cl = train$region, k = 3))
  data.frame(calibration = cal, test_animals = length(unique(test$animal)), test_spectra = nrow(test),
             accuracy_index = mean(pred_index == test$region), accuracy_model = mean(pred_model == test$region))
}
comparison <- rbind(evaluate("matching"), evaluate("stale"))
stopifnot(length(intersect(unique(train$animal), unique(spectra$animal[spectra$week == 2]))) == 0)
comparison
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>   calibration test_animals test_spectra accuracy_index accuracy_model
#> 1    matching            4           24            1.0      0.9166667
#> 2       stale            4           24            0.5      0.5000000
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
stopifnot(comparison$accuracy_index[1] >= comparison$accuracy_model[1],   # the model does not beat the index
          comparison$accuracy_index[2] == 0.5, comparison$accuracy_model[2] == 0.5)
```
:::


With the matching calibration, the index classifies 100% of the
24 test spectra correctly and the model 92%.
The more flexible model brings no gain here, so the index remains the reference method in the model passport
(@sec-b27). With the stale calibration both drop to 50%: every flap tip now looks like a flap base. A learning model
does not repair an illumination error; it learns on top of it. The independent test denominator is four animals, not
24 spectra.

::: {.callout-note title="Other implementation: Python with scikit-image and PyTorch"}
Hyperspectral pipelines are often written in Python. [scikit-image](https://scikit-image.org/docs/stable/) (version
0.26.0 in November 2026) provides tested image operators such as filtering, registration and region measurements;
most of them accept a `channel_axis` argument, and for a cube stored as rows × columns × bands this must be set to the
spectral axis, otherwise the filter mixes neighbouring wavelengths [@vanderwalt2014skimage]. PyTorch connects to
pretrained networks [@paszke2019pytorch]. Networks with ImageNet weights, as in the [transfer learning
tutorial](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/transfer_learning_tutorial.html), expect three colour channels
normalised with ImageNet means; a 101-band cube needs a new first layer, whose weights then cannot be transferred.
Pretrained hyperspectral weights from research code are only usable if wavelength grid, calibration (reflectance, not
raw counts), spatial resolution and band order match. For a fair comparison with this lab, both implementations must
receive the identical calibrated reflectance table, the same animal-wise split (week-1 animals for development,
week-2 animals for testing), the same index definition and the same accuracy computed per spectrum and per animal.
Status: conceptual comparison, not run.
:::

## Counter-check {#sec-b10-countercheck}

Predict first, then compute. Suppose the replacement lamp had been only brighter, with exactly the same spectral shape
as the original. Would the stale white reference still inflate the index? And would the grey check tile still fail?


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(3010)
lamp_C <- 1.2 * lamp_A                                  # brighter only, same spectral shape
raw_tip <- raw_counts(tissue_reflectance(0.45, 1.5), lamp_C)
index_stale_brightness <- oxygen_index(calibrate(raw_tip, white_ref$week1))
grey_C <- rowMeans(calibrate(sapply(1:100, function(i) raw_counts(rep(0.5, length(wl)), lamp_C)), white_ref$week1))
c(true_index = oxygen_index(tissue_reflectance(0.45, 1.5)),
  stale_reference_brighter_lamp = index_stale_brightness,
  grey_index = oxygen_index(grey_C), grey_mean_reflectance = mean(grey_C))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>                    true_index stale_reference_brighter_lamp 
#>                     0.7499384                     0.7407447 
#>                    grey_index         grey_mean_reflectance 
#>                     1.0003271                     0.6001668
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
stopifnot(abs(index_stale_brightness / oxygen_index(tissue_reflectance(0.45, 1.5)) - 1) < 0.03,
          abs(oxygen_index(grey_C) - 1) <= 0.02, mean(grey_C) > 0.55)
```
:::


The ratio index survives a pure change in brightness: it stays within a few per cent of the true value, and the grey
tile's index stays within tolerance. The grey tile's mean reflectance, however, rises to about
0.60 instead of 0.50, so the check still flags a problem with absolute reflectance. A
change in the lamp's colour affects the index; a change in brightness affects absolute values. The grey tile should be
read on both quantities.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"A ratio index needs no calibration." A ratio cancels everything that scales all wavelengths alike, such as distance,
exposure time or a brighter lamp of the same colour. It does not cancel anything that changes the spectral shape: a
new lamp type, an ageing bulb, daylight from a window or a different filter. A white reference recorded under the
actual light remains necessary.
:::

A design counter-check needs no code: if animals of both groups had been imaged in alternating order in both weeks,
as ARRIVE item 4b recommends for the order of measurements [@percie2020arrive], the lamp change would have shifted both
groups alike and could not have produced a group difference.

## Consequences for patients and operations {#sec-b10-consequences}

**Wrong tissue interpretation.** The same artefact in a clinical setting would make poorly oxygenated tissue look
better oxygenated than it is. A surgeon judging a flap by such a value might delay a revision. The measurement
assumption that protects against this is checkable: *a grey reference tile imaged at every session has an index of
1.00 ± 0.02 and a mean reflectance of 0.50 ± 0.01*. The failure mode is equally concrete: a lamp change without a new
white reference shifts every index of that session by the same factor.

**Animals and the 3Rs.** A false positive treatment effect in an animal study has consequences beyond the abstract. It
invites follow-up experiments, and therefore more animals, to pursue an effect that was never there. Reduction in the
sense of the 3Rs starts with analyses that use the animal as the unit and designs that avoid confounding
[@nc3rs3rs]. Reporting the experimental unit and the order of measurements is part of ARRIVE [@percie2020arrive].

**Regulation.** In this preclinical study the camera is a research instrument. If the same index were offered to
clinicians to assess flap perfusion, its intended purpose would decide whether the software is a medical device and
which class applies; @sec-b22 works through such an intended purpose.

**Data protection and security.** Animal data are not personal data. In a human study, wound and skin images can
show tattoos, faces or rare findings and become identifiable; @sec-b23 covers this. The white reference and
calibration files are part of the measurement. Storing them with a version and a checksum, so that the analysis can
prove which file it used, is an integrity control of the kind discussed in @sec-b24.

## Look up and transfer {#sec-b10-lookup}

- **Reviewer question:** The manuscript reports p < 0.001 for a difference in an oxygenation index between two groups
  of animals. What was the experimental unit, were both groups imaged in the same sessions, and which reference target
  shows that the calibration was stable across sessions?
- **Self-test:** A follow-up study images six animals per group, with four acquisitions per animal and 50 pixels per
  region of interest. A colleague proposes to divide every spectrum by its own mean, "to remove the lamp". How many
  independent units does the group comparison have, does the proposal remove a change in lamp colour, and which design
  change prevents the confounding in this chapter?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The group comparison has 12 independent units, six animals per group; the 2,400 pixels per region and the 48
acquisitions are repeated measurements within animals. Dividing by the mean removes a change in brightness but not a
change in spectral shape, so a lamp with a different colour still distorts the ratio $R(660)/R(800)$; only a white
reference recorded under the same lamp corrects it. Imaging animals of both groups in alternating or randomised order
within every session prevents the lamp from coinciding with the group, and a grey reference tile at every session
detects a calibration problem before any animal is analysed.
:::
